claims.text: The starting materials are crystalline, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles composed of five or more metals.
Tungsten and molybdenum are refractory metals.
A small addition of tungsten or molybdenum can overcome structural or chemical instability of the nanoparticles at 773–1173 K.
Adding another metallic constituent increases the configurational entropy of a multicomponent alloy.
A tungsten or molybdenum addition will produce a stable solid solution in the nanoparticles.
Increased configurational entropy stabilizes disordered solid-solution phases relative to ordered intermetallic phases.
Entropy-driven solid-solution stabilization reduces both structural and chemical instability during catalytic operation.
Refractory-metal-modified nanoparticles will be more stable and degradation-resistant than otherwise identical nanoparticles without the addition.
The proposed operating and testing temperature range is 773–1173 K.
X-ray diffraction, transmission electron microscopy, and energy-dispersive spectroscopy will be used to monitor structure and composition during thermal exposure.
Observation of significant structural or chemical instability in the modified nanoparticles would falsify the hypothesis.
